title: Watt's Sunday Walk
summary: A young Scottish instrument maker was asked to fix a tiny model engine that kept stopping. He measured everything and discovered the engine was wasting most of its steam heating and cooling itself. On a Sunday walk he had a brilliant idea: cool the steam in a separate box so the cylinder could stay hot!

sections.heading: A Quiet Boy from Greenock
paragraphs: Picture a busy harbour town on the River Clyde in the west of Scotland in the 1740s. Tall-masted ships creak at the quays, ropes slap against wood, and the air smells of tar, salt and fresh-cut timber. This is Greenock, and in a house not far from the water lives a small, thin boy who often has headaches and is frequently kept home from school because he is unwell. His name is James Watt, and he was born here on 19 January 1736.

James's father, also called James Watt, was a shipwright, which means a builder and repairer of ships. He also traded goods, owned shares in ships, and helped run the town as one of its officials. His workshop was full of tools, wood, metal fittings and the delicate navigation instruments that sailors relied on to find their way across the ocean. His mother, Agnes Muirhead, came from a well-educated family and taught him a great deal at home. Because young James was so often ill, much of his early learning happened at the kitchen table and in his father's workshop rather than in a classroom.

That workshop turned out to be a perfect school. James was given his own small set of tools and a little forge, and he took things apart and put them back together: models, cranes, pulleys, barrel organs. Family stories say he was quiet, patient and unusually good at mathematics once he got to grammar school. He liked to understand exactly why things worked, not just that they worked. Hold on to that habit, because it is the real hero of this chapter.

Life was not easy for the Watt family. Several of James's brothers and sisters died young, which was sadly common in the 1700s, and his father's business ran into money trouble when some trading ventures failed. When James was still a teenager, his mother died. A teenager who was good with his hands needed a trade, and James decided on one that matched his talents perfectly: he would become a maker of mathematical instruments.

What was a mathematical instrument maker? Today we might call it a precision engineer. These craftspeople built quadrants and sextants for navigation, compasses, surveying tools, drawing instruments, scales, rulers marked with tiny accurate divisions, and scientific apparatus for universities. The work needed steady hands, sharp eyes, careful measuring and a deep understanding of geometry. All of those skills would matter enormously when Watt later faced a giant, clumsy, wasteful machine and asked how to make it better.

sections.heading: London Lessons and a Workshop in a University
paragraphs: In 1755, aged 19, Watt travelled to London, a long and tiring journey that took more than a week on horseback. London was the biggest city in Europe, with hundreds of thousands of people, and it was the best place in Britain to learn the instrument-making trade. The problem was that the craft was controlled by guilds, organisations of master craftsmen who normally expected a young person to serve a long apprenticeship of about seven years before working independently.

Watt did not have seven years, or much money. After some searching, he found a master, an instrument maker named John Morgan in Cornhill, who agreed to teach him for about a year in return for a fee and his labour. Watt worked extremely long days, often from early morning until late at night, learning to cut brass, engrave fine scales and build complicated instruments. He lived very cheaply and kept out of sight as much as possible, partly because in wartime young men on the streets of London could be grabbed by press gangs and forced into the navy. The hard work and cold, cheap lodgings damaged his health, and in 1756 he returned to Scotland, tired but highly skilled.

Back in Scotland he wanted to set up shop in Glasgow, the growing trading city upriver from Greenock. According to the traditional account, Glasgow's own craft guild objected: Watt had not served a full apprenticeship, so in their eyes he was not entitled to open a business in the town (historians still debate how strongly the guild really opposed him). This might have stopped his career right there. Instead, a lucky escape appeared. The University of Glasgow was not under the control of the town guild, and some of its professors needed someone to care for a collection of astronomical instruments that had recently arrived from Jamaica.

In 1757 the university gave Watt a small workshop inside its buildings and allowed him to call himself mathematical instrument maker to the university. He repaired and built instruments, sold drawing tools and spectacles, and even made musical instruments such as flutes and organs, even though he was not especially musical himself. He simply studied the science of sound and worked it out.

Being inside a university turned out to be even more valuable than the workshop itself. Watt's little room became a meeting place for curious minds. Among his friends were the chemist and doctor Joseph Black, the student (and later professor) John Robison, and the philosopher Adam Smith, who would go on to write The Wealth of Nations, a famous book about economics. Imagine a small, cluttered room full of brass tubes, glass, half-finished instruments and lively conversation about heat, chemistry, mathematics and trade. That was the world in which Watt's great idea would grow.

sections.heading: A Little Broken Engine
paragraphs: The university owned a small working model of a Newcomen engine, the kind of atmospheric engine you met in Part 6, which pumped water out of mines using a rocking beam, a piston and the push of the air. Professors used the model to show students how a real engine worked. Unfortunately, this one hardly worked at all. It had even been sent away to London to be fixed, and it came back still disappointing.

In the winter of 1763 to 1764, the professor of natural philosophy, John Anderson, asked Watt to repair it. Watt was about 27. The model was small, roughly the size of a tabletop machine: by most accounts its brass cylinder was only about 5 centimetres (2 inches) across, and its piston moved about 15 centimetres (6 inches) each stroke. Everything else was in proportion, with a little boiler, a little beam and little pump rods.

Watt cleaned it, adjusted it, and got it going. But he found that even when properly repaired, the engine would make only a few strokes and then stop. The boiler simply could not make steam fast enough to keep it running, even though the boiler looked big enough compared with the size of the cylinder. Many people would have shrugged, written it off as a toy that does not scale down well, and handed it back. Watt did not. Something about the numbers bothered him.

He started measuring. He worked out how much water the boiler turned into steam each minute, and how much steam it should take to fill the cylinder once. The answer was startling. The engine was using several times more steam per stroke than the volume of the cylinder could possibly hold. Steam was disappearing. Where on earth was it going?

This is a wonderful moment in the history of invention, because it shows a kind of thinking that anyone can learn. Watt did not start with a grand plan to change the world. He started with a small, specific question about a machine on a workbench: why does this little engine stall, and why do the measurements not add up? Following that question carefully, step by step, would lead him to one of the most important improvements in the history of engineering.

sections.heading: Hot, Cold, Hot, Cold: Where the Fuel Went
paragraphs: To find the missing steam, remember how a Newcomen engine works. Steam fills the cylinder. Then a spray of cold water is squirted inside. The steam condenses (turns back into a few drops of water), leaving a near-vacuum, and the air outside pushes the piston down. Then fresh steam comes in for the next stroke.

Now think about the cylinder itself. Every time the cold spray goes in, it does not only cool the steam. It also cools the metal walls of the cylinder and the piston. So when the next lot of steam arrives, the first thing it meets is a chilly cylinder. Much of that new steam immediately condenses on the cold walls, warming them back up, before the cylinder is hot enough to stay full of steam. Only after the cylinder has been reheated can steam fill it properly. Then the spray cools everything again, and the whole wasteful cycle repeats, ten or twelve times every minute, all day and all night.

Watt realised that most of the steam, and therefore most of the coal burned under the boiler, was being used not to work the engine but simply to reheat the cylinder over and over. In his little model the problem was even worse than in a big engine, because a small cylinder has a lot of metal surface compared with the amount of steam inside it. He estimated that around three quarters of the steam was being wasted this way.

He tried the obvious fixes first. He experimented with making cylinders out of materials that do not soak up heat so easily, including wood treated with oil, so that the walls would not need as much reheating. That helped a little but created other problems. He also tried using less cold water in the spray, so that the cylinder did not cool down so much. But then the steam did not condense completely, the vacuum was weak, and the piston was pushed down with much less force.

Here was the puzzle in its sharpest form. For a strong vacuum, the place where steam condenses must be cold. For no wasted fuel, the cylinder must stay hot. One part of the machine seemed to need to be hot and cold at the same time. Every engineer who had built Newcomen engines for the past fifty years had lived with this contradiction. Watt was the one who decided it must be possible to escape from it.

sections.heading: Joseph Black and the Hidden Heat
paragraphs: While Watt puzzled over his engine, he had an expert friend just down the corridor. Joseph Black, born in 1728, was a doctor and chemist who taught at the University of Glasgow. He is famous in chemistry for studying the gas he called fixed air, which we now call carbon dioxide. But it was Black's work on heat that mattered most to Watt.

Around 1761, Black noticed something odd. If you heat a block of ice that is sitting at its melting point, its temperature does not go up while it melts. All the heat you pour in goes into turning solid ice into liquid water. The same thing happens when water boils: you can keep heating boiling water, but its temperature stays at the boiling point while it slowly turns into steam. The heat seems to vanish into the water without showing up on a thermometer. Black called this heat latent, from a Latin word meaning hidden. Latent heat is the hidden heat needed to turn boiling water into steam without making it any hotter.

Black also studied what we now call specific heat: the idea that different substances need different amounts of heat to warm up by the same number of degrees. Together, these ideas helped scientists see that heat and temperature are not the same thing. Temperature is how hot something is; heat is a quantity of energy that can flow, be stored, and even hide.

Watt, meanwhile, was doing experiments of his own. In one of them he led steam from a kettle-like boiler through a tube into a container of cold water and measured how much the water warmed up. He was amazed to find that a small amount of steam could heat about six times its own weight of cold water all the way up to boiling. Steam was carrying an enormous load of heat, far more than its temperature suggested. When he told Black, his friend explained his theory of latent heat, and the surprising result suddenly made sense.

Watt also measured how much bigger steam is than the water it comes from, getting, by one account, a figure of roughly 1,800 times by volume, close to the modern value of about 1,700 times at normal air pressure. With these numbers he could calculate how much fuel an engine ought to need, and compare it with how much it actually used. The gap was huge. Black's science gave Watt a way to understand exactly why the Newcomen engine was so hungry: every time the cold spray condensed steam inside the cylinder, all that hidden heat was thrown away, and then had to be put back in again by burning more coal.

Black did more than share ideas. He became a loyal supporter of Watt's engine research and lent him money for his experiments in the early years. Historians still discuss exactly how much Black's theory shaped Watt's breakthrough; Watt himself said he had noticed the effect in his own experiments and that Black then explained it to him. Either way, it is a lovely example of a scientist and a craftsman learning from each other.

sections.heading: The Sunday Walk on Glasgow Green
paragraphs: Now comes the famous moment. On a fine Sunday afternoon in May 1765, Watt went for a walk across Glasgow Green, a large open park beside the River Clyde where townspeople strolled, washed and dried their linen, and grazed animals. In strict Scotland of the 1700s, Sunday was a day of rest, so he could not go to his workshop. Instead his mind kept turning over the problem of the hot-and-cold cylinder.

As he walked, an idea arrived. Steam is elastic, he reasoned: like any gas, it will rush into an empty space. So if there were a separate vessel, joined to the cylinder by a pipe and emptied of air, steam from the cylinder would rush into it. If that separate vessel were kept cold, the steam would condense there, creating a vacuum. And that vacuum would pull more steam out of the cylinder, emptying the cylinder too. The cylinder itself never needed to be cooled at all.

In other words: do the condensing somewhere else. Keep the cylinder hot all the time, and keep a second chamber, the condenser, cold all the time. Hot stays hot, cold stays cold, and the contradiction disappears. Watt later said that before he had walked much further, the whole arrangement was clear in his mind.

We know about this walk mainly because Watt described it to friends many years later, and their account was written down after his death. So, as the story outline for this Deep Dive says, it is how Watt later remembered it, and memories can tidy up the past. But unlike the kettle legend, this account comes from Watt himself, and it fits what we know from his notes and models. The date, 1765, is widely accepted.

Watt was eager to test the idea immediately, but he had to wait for Monday. Soon afterwards he built a small experimental model. Stories say he used a large brass syringe as the cylinder, a quick and clever way to try out the principle without making new parts. The model worked. With a separate condenser, a small cylinder could make stroke after stroke with far less steam than before.

sections.heading: Condenser, Air Pump, Jacket: Building the Better Engine
paragraphs: A good idea is not the same as a working machine, and Watt soon found there was more to solve. First, the condenser would gradually fill up with the water from condensed steam, plus the cold water used to cool it, plus air that leaked in or came out of the water. Water and air in the condenser would spoil the vacuum. So Watt added an air pump: a small pump, worked by the engine itself, that pulled the warm water and air out of the condenser at every stroke. The warm water could even be sent back to the boiler, saving a little more fuel because it was already partly heated.

Second, in a Newcomen engine the top of the cylinder was open to the air. Cold air resting on top of the piston cooled the cylinder every stroke. Watt closed the top of the cylinder with a cover, letting the piston rod slide through a tight seal. Then, instead of using the weight of the atmosphere to push the piston down, he used low-pressure steam from the boiler to push on top of it, while the condenser created a vacuum underneath. This was a big step: steam now did some of the pushing, although at fairly low pressure.

Third, he wrapped the cylinder in a steam jacket: an outer case around the cylinder, filled with steam, like a warm coat. With hot steam all around it, the cylinder walls stayed close to steam temperature, so less steam condensed on them by mistake. He also tried lagging, or insulating, parts of the engine with materials such as wood to keep the heat in.

Put together, the separate condenser, the air pump, the closed cylinder and the steam jacket made a very different machine from Newcomen's, even though it still looked like a beam engine with a rocking beam and a pump. Fully developed, Watt's engines used roughly a quarter of the coal of a Newcomen engine doing the same work. For a mine owner who had to pay for coal, that was like discovering that three out of every four sacks of fuel had been thrown away for decades.

Building a full-size engine, though, was a struggle. Watt needed money for materials and time. In the late 1760s he found a backer, the Scottish industrialist John Roebuck, who had founded the Carron ironworks and who was struggling with flooded coal mines of his own near Bo'ness. Roebuck paid off Watt's debts, including money owed to Joseph Black, in exchange for a large share of the future invention. Watt built a test engine in a workshop beside Roebuck's home, Kinneil House, near Bo'ness on the Firth of Forth. The ruin of that little workshop still survives.

On 5 January 1769 Watt was granted his famous patent, for, as its title put it, a new method of lessening the consumption of steam and fuel in fire engines. (Fire engine was the old name for a steam engine.) A patent gave him the right, for a limited time, to stop others from using his invention without permission. The idea was protected. But the engine at Kinneil still did not work properly. Its cylinder was not round and smooth enough, and steam hissed out around the edges of the piston, which Watt tried to seal with materials such as cork, oiled rags, felt and even horse dung, with little success.

sections.heading: The Kettle Legend, and Giving Fair Credit
paragraphs: You may have heard a different story about James Watt. In it, a young Watt sits by the fire at home, staring at a boiling kettle, and watches the lid jiggle as steam escapes. An aunt scolds him for wasting time, but in that moment, the story says, he realises the power of steam and goes on to invent the steam engine.

It is a charming scene, and it has appeared in countless books and paintings. But it is a legend. There is no good evidence that it happened, and the story seems to have grown up after Watt's death; it may even have been created or embellished by his son, James Watt Junior, to polish his father's legend. The truth is more interesting. Watt did use kettles, but as pieces of scientific apparatus in measured experiments on how much heat steam carried, not as a sudden flash of inspiration from a rattling lid. And his great insight came not as a child, but as a grown man of 29, after months of careful measuring.

The other half of the myth is even more important to correct. James Watt did not invent the steam engine. Steam pumps had been working since Savery's time around 1700, and Newcomen's atmospheric engines had been pumping mines since 1712, more than fifty years before Watt's walk on Glasgow Green. What Watt invented was a way to make the steam engine far more efficient, starting with the separate condenser. Efficiency means how much of the fuel's energy becomes useful work instead of wasted heat, and Watt's changes improved it dramatically.

That might sound like a smaller achievement than inventing the whole thing, but it is not. An idea that cuts fuel use by about three quarters can turn a machine that only makes sense next to a coal mine into one that can be used almost anywhere. Over the next decades, Watt and his partners would keep improving the engine in many other ways, which you will meet in Parts 8 and 9.

So the fair way to tell this story is to say that the steam engine was built by many people over a long time: Papin with his piston idea, Savery with his pump, Newcomen and Calley with the first practical engine, Black with his science of heat, and Watt with his brilliant, patient improvements. Watt's real lesson for young inventors is not to stare at kettles. It is to notice waste, measure carefully, ask why the numbers do not add up, and keep thinking about a problem until the answer arrives, even on a Sunday stroll.

And yet, in 1769, Watt's story seemed stuck. He had a patent, a brilliant idea and a test engine that leaked. He had no money of his own, no proper factory, and no way to make a large cylinder accurate enough to hold its steam. He took jobs surveying routes for canals in Scotland to earn a living, and his engine sat waiting. Then, through friends, he came to know a lively, ambitious businessman in Birmingham who owned one of the most famous factories in Britain, and who believed that Watt's engine could change the world.

deepDive: Why was the Newcomen engine so wasteful, and how much did Watt really save? Modern numbers make the problem clear. Heating 1 kilogram of water from 0 °C to 100 °C takes about 419 kilojoules of energy, but turning that same kilogram of boiling water into steam takes about 2,260 kilojoules more: the latent heat Joseph Black described. So most of the energy in steam is hidden heat, and in a Newcomen engine it was thrown away every stroke when the cold spray hit the cylinder. Watt's own experiment, in which steam heated about six times its weight of cold water to boiling, matches this well: 2,260 divided by roughly 400 is between five and six. The cylinder walls made it worse. A large cast-iron cylinder weighs tonnes, and cooling and reheating even its inner surface ten or twelve times a minute swallowed steam that never pushed the piston at all. Watt estimated that about three quarters of the steam in his small model was wasted this way. His solution is a beautiful example of separating functions: one part of the machine (the cylinder) stays as hot as the steam, while another (the condenser) stays as cold as possible. The air pump keeps the condenser free of water and air, which would otherwise spoil the vacuum. In thermodynamic terms, Watt reduced the losses that come from heat flowing back and forth inside the engine, decades before Sadi Carnot (Part 16) wrote the theory down. Historians still debate how much Black's science drove Watt's invention. Watt credited Black generously, but he also said he found the key facts through his own measurements and only then learned Black's theory. Many historians now see it as a two-way exchange between university science and craft skill, rather than a simple case of theory being applied. Another debate concerns the Glasgow Green story itself. It reached print through recollections recorded long after 1765, so details like the exact spot may have been polished. But Watt's notebooks and early models confirm the timing broadly. Finally, the efficiency gain: fully developed Watt engines used roughly a quarter of the coal of comparable Newcomen engines. Yet in absolute terms they were still inefficient, turning only a few percent of the coal's energy into useful work. There was plenty of room left for later engineers.
funFact: Watt's first test of the separate condenser idea is said to have used a large brass syringe as its cylinder, and an early model of his separate condenser is kept today at the Science Museum in London.
